title: break and continue
description: Leave a loop early, or skip a single turn, without changing its condition.

content.value: Sometimes you know halfway through a turn that there is no point carrying on. `break` ends the loop at once. The program carries on below the loop.

steps.note: The loop is written to count to 10.
`break`: the rest of the body is skipped and the condition is never tested again.
Only the loop ended, not the program.

content.title: Watch break stop the loop

content.value: You met `break` in a `switch` in Module 4, where it stops cases falling through. In a loop it does the matching job: it ends the thing it is inside.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: When `i` is 4, `break` runs before the print. So only 1, 2 and 3 are printed.

content.value: `continue` is gentler. It abandons the current turn only, jumps to the next one, and leaves the loop running.

content.title: break vs continue
content.caption: In a `for` loop, the update `i++` still runs after a `continue`, so the loop moves on safely.
An `if (i % 3 != 0)` around the print would do the same. `continue` earns its place when the rest of the body is long: the guard sits at the top and the real work stays flat.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: On even turns, `continue` skips the print. The loop keeps going, so only the odd numbers appear.

content.value: The commonest use of `break` is a search. Look for the first thing that matches. Once you have it, there is nothing left to look for.

content.caption: Sample run: type 91 and it reports `91 divides by 7` at once, without testing up to 90. Type 97 and the loop runs out: `97 is prime.`

content.value: After the loop, the counter alone cannot tell you whether you left early or ran out. So you leave yourself a note: a `bool` **flag** like `found`, set just before the `break`.
content.title: Why the flag?

content.value: `while (true)` is true for ever, so the only way out is a `break` inside. This lets you read the input once, at the top, and test it in the middle.

content.title: One turn of the loop below
content.caption: This is the sentinel loop from the `while` lesson, without the duplicated read.
Sample run: 5, -2, 3, 0 prints `Ignoring -2` then `Total: 8`. Keep one clear exit near the top: a loop with scattered breaks is hard to read.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `n` goes 5, 10, 15. Only at 15 is `n > 12` true, so `break` runs and 15 is printed.

content.value: In a `while` loop the update is just a line in the body. A `continue` skips the rest of the body, and that can include your update.

content.title: continue and the update
content.caption: If a loop seems frozen on one value, look for a `continue` that jumps over the update. Update before you skip, or use a `for` loop.
The second trap: `break` leaves only the loop it is written in. With a loop inside a loop, the outer one carries on as normal.

content.value: To leave both loops at once, set a `bool` flag and test it in the outer loop's condition too. It is the clearest way, and the one you will see most often.

quiz.question: What does `break` do inside a loop?
options: Ends the loop at once and carries on with the line after it
Skips the current turn and starts the next one
quiz.explain: The condition is never tested again. The program continues below the loop, not at the end of main.

quiz.question: What does `continue` do?
options: Abandons the current turn only and moves on to the next one
Restarts the loop from its first value
quiz.explain: The rest of the block is skipped for that turn, then the loop carries on as normal.

quiz.question: Why does a search loop often need a `bool found` as well as a `break`?
options: Because break does not work without it
To stop the loop running twice
After the loop you cannot otherwise tell whether you found something or ran out
quiz.explain: Both endings leave the loop the same way, so the flag is the note you left yourself about which one happened.

quiz.question: Why can `continue` freeze a `while` loop but not a `for` loop?
options: In a while loop the update is a line in the block, and continue skips the rest of the block
while loops test their condition less often
continue is not allowed in a for loop
quiz.explain: A `for` loop's update lives in the brackets and runs on every turn regardless. In a `while`, if the update sits after the `continue`, it never happens.

quiz.question: A `break` inside the inner of two nested loops does what?
options: Leaves the inner loop only: the outer loop carries on
quiz.explain: It ends the loop it was written in. Use a bool flag tested by the outer condition if you need to leave both.
